questions_and_answers.question_text: What always precedes specifiers in Chinese?
What usually precedes specifiers in Chinese?
How does this compare with English word order?
Write the Chinese for "this teacup of yours."
Write the Chinese for "those dishes I bought."
Which two elements are being compared in this note?

answers.answer_text: Possessives and modifying clauses, both relative to specifiers.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "I didn't buy the expensive ones."
Write the Chinese for "It was bought at the First Company too."

answers.answer_text: Yě shi zài Dìyī Gōngsī mǎide.

questions_and_answers.question_text: In Guìde wǒ méi mǎi, what position does the object occupy?

answers.answer_text: Topic position, at the beginning of the sentence.

articles.text:
9.  B: Tāmen màide pánziwǎn, yǒude   Some of the dishes they sell are
       zhēn hǎokàn. Kěshi guì         really beautiful. But they are
       yìdiǎn.                        a little expensive.

10. B: Wǒ mǎide nàxie pánziwǎn dōu   All those dishes I bought were not
       bú tài guì. Guìde wǒ méi       too expensive. I didn't buy the
       mǎi.                           expensive ones.

11. B: Nǐde zhèige chábēi hěn hǎo.   This teacup of yours is very nice.
       Shi zài shénme dìfang          Where was it bought?
       mǎide?
    A: Yě shi zài Dìyī Gōngsī         It was bought at the First Company
       mǎide.                         too.

Notes on Nos. 10-11

Nǐde zhèige chábēi, wǒ mǎide nàxie pánziwǎn: Possessives always precede specifiers in Chinese, and modifying clauses usually precede specifiers. This is the opposite of English word order for the same elements. Compare:

nǐde        |  zhèige   |  chábēi        (this teacup of yours)
wǒ mǎide    |  nàxie    |  pánziwǎn      (those dishes I bought)
